newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban decree Islamic ways in north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban decree Islamic ways in north.

text.p: The Taleban militia went on spreading its strict Islamic rule across Afghanistan on Monday, announcing restrictions on living in the newly captured northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif.

The Taleban leader, Mullah Abdul Razzaq, and General Abdul Malik, whose mutiny against ousted opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum led to the fall of the city on Saturday, addressed a large crowd at the imposing Hazrat Ali mosque.

"There are no differences between the ethnic groups of Afghanistan," said Razzaq, the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban's top figure on a joint eight-man military council with Malik's ethnic Uzbek forces.

An announcer read out four new rules, decreeing that people should reopen their shops, women should wear the all-enveloping Burqa robe, women should stop working outside their homes and girls should stop going to school or university.

The regulations are in line with those imposed in Kabul and other Taleban-controlled parts of Afghanistan where the Islamic militia has also ordered men to grow long beards and banned music, videos and most other forms of entertainment.
In deference to the Taleban's new Uzbek allies, few of whom are bearded, no rules for facial hair were announced.
Malik later held talks with Pakistani ambassador Aziz Khan, who flew to Mazar-i-Sharif a day after his country became the first to recognise the Taleban administration in Kabul.

"Afghanistan is very important neighbour. We would like peace to be established here so that Afghanistan can go ahead with its task of economic reconstruction and all the refugees we have played host to in Pakistan for such a long time can return home," Khan told reporters after the meeting.
He said turmoil in Afghanistan had prevented economic development, including construction of oil and gas pipelines from Turkmenistan across Afghanistan to Pakistan.
"Afghanistan occupies a very important position regarding access from central Asian republics to the Indian Ocean via Afghanistan and Pakistan," he said.
"Hopefully, once peace comes, those pipelines would be laid, roads will be constructed and we will have trade and access to the Central Asian republics," he added.
Khan urged other countries, which have so far shown reluctance to recognise the Taleban rule, to follow Pakistan's lead and acknowledge "ground realities".
He said Pakistani consulate staff in Mazar-i-Sharif, evacuated two days ago just before Dostum lost control of the city, had returned on Monday, adding: "So I thought I would hitch a ride."
Khan said Pakistan had limited resources but would offer whatever help it could to "our brothers in Afghanistan".
Pakistan has long denied charges it supports the Taleban.
Khan voiced confidence that the Afghan government would be broad-based and represent all ethnic minorities.
Taleban fighters with black beards and turbans roamed Mazar-i-Sharif on Monday, establishing a highly visible presence in this former opposition stronghold.

Taleban troops, armed with rocket-propelled grenades and rifles, patrolled the northern capital, which was calm, though a few distant explosions could be heard. There was no immediate report on their cause.
Civilian men walked or cycled through the streets, gaping curiously at the 2,500 Taleban fighters who swept into the city on Sunday night.
Hardly any private cars were to be seen and mule-drawn carts provided the only form of public transport.
Foreign aid workers were keeping a low profile staying in their homes and offices for the time being.
"We have had no security incidents since Taleban arrived," one aid worker said, adding that Malik's forces had recovered two of three vehicles stolen in the chaos when the city fell.

Malik, who joined forces with the Taleban after staging his anti-Dostum mutiny a week ago, announced that Islamic Sharia law would be applied in the north, saying girls and women would be excluded from schools and universities until there was enough money to build segregated facilities.
Very few women were to be seen on the streets on Monday and a few who ventured out were wearing Burqa.
"I am not too worried about the Taleban now," said one taxi driver. "But when they get full control of the city, we may have problems playing music in the car."
